title: Git Essentials
description: Staging and diffs, branches, fast-forward vs merge commits, conflicts, merge vs rebase, remotes, stash, amend, reset modes, revert, cherry-pick, reflog, tags, history inspection, worktrees.

cards.title: `git init` vs `git clone <url>`: what does each one do?
cards.body:
`git init` creates a new, empty repository; `git clone` copies an existing one with its full history.

`git init` creates a `.git` directory in the current folder. `git clone` also sets up a remote named `origin` pointing at the source and checks out the default branch.

Tip: `git clone <url>` creates a new folder named after the repository unless you give it a folder name.
cards.searchQuery: git init vs git clone difference

cards.title: Which command stages a file's current changes so they're included in the next commit?
cards.body:
`git add <path>`

The **staging area** (index) is a snapshot of what the next commit will contain. `git commit` records only what is staged.

Tip: `git status` shows staged vs unstaged changes, and `git add -p` stages individual hunks.
cards.searchQuery: git add stage changes staging area

cards.title: Which command shows the changes you've staged but not yet committed?
cards.body:
`git diff --staged`

It compares the index with `HEAD`. The synonym is `--cached`.

Watch out: plain `git diff` compares the working tree with the index, so it shows only **unstaged** changes. `git diff HEAD` shows staged and unstaged together.
cards.searchQuery: git diff staged cached changes

cards.title: A file is already tracked by Git. Does adding its name to `.gitignore` stop Git from tracking changes to it?
cards.body:
No

`.gitignore` only affects **untracked** files. Once a file is tracked, Git keeps tracking it.

Example: to stop tracking an accidentally committed `.env` file but keep it on disk, run `git rm --cached .env`, then commit.

Watch out: the old versions stay in history; removing a leaked secret from the repo does not make it safe.
cards.searchQuery: gitignore already tracked file git rm cached

cards.title: One command to create a new branch named `feature` and switch to it?
cards.body:
`git switch -c feature`

The older equivalent is `git checkout -b feature`.

Watch out: `git branch feature` only creates the branch; you stay on the current one. Move between existing branches with `git switch <name>`.
cards.searchQuery: git switch -c create and switch branch

cards.title: When does `git merge` fast-forward instead of creating a merge commit?
cards.body:
When the current branch's tip is an **ancestor** of the branch being merged.

That means your branch has no commits the other lacks, so Git just moves the branch pointer forward.

If both sides have new commits, Git creates a merge commit with two parents.

Tip: `--no-ff` forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible.
cards.searchQuery: git merge fast-forward vs merge commit

cards.title: In a merge conflict, what do the sections between `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` contain?
cards.body:
From `<<<<<<<` to `=======` is your **current branch's** version; from `=======` to `>>>>>>>` is the **incoming** branch's version.

Edit to the final content and delete every marker. Then `git add` the file and run `git commit` (or `git merge --continue`).

Watch out: during a rebase the sides swap. The top part (`HEAD`) is the branch you're rebasing onto, and the bottom part is your commit being replayed.
cards.searchQuery: git merge conflict markers HEAD incoming

cards.title: Merge vs rebase: how does each integrate another branch's work, and what's the golden rule of rebasing?
cards.body:
Merge ties histories together with a merge commit; rebase replays your commits on top of the other branch.

Merge leaves existing commits untouched. Rebase creates **new commits with new hashes**, giving a linear history.

Watch out: **never rebase commits others already have** (pushed, shared). It rewrites history they've built on.
cards.searchQuery: git merge vs rebase golden rule

cards.title: Which command downloads new commits from a remote without changing your current branch or working tree?
cards.body:
`git fetch`

It only updates remote-tracking branches such as `origin/main`.

`git pull` is `git fetch` followed by integrating the fetched commits into your current branch (fast-forward, merge, or rebase with `--rebase`).

Tip: fetch first when you want to inspect incoming changes before integrating them.
cards.searchQuery: git fetch vs git pull difference

cards.title: Command to reapply your most recently stashed changes and remove that entry from the stash list?
cards.body:
`git stash pop`

`git stash apply` reapplies the changes but keeps the entry.

Watch out: if `pop` hits a conflict, the entry is kept. Remove it with `git stash drop` after resolving.

Tip: `git stash -u` also stashes untracked files.
cards.searchQuery: git stash pop reapply stashed changes

cards.title: Command that replaces your most recent commit, e.g. to fix its message or add a forgotten staged file?
cards.body:
`git commit --amend`

It creates a **new commit** (new hash) that replaces the old one.

Watch out: amending is fine before pushing. Amending a commit that is already pushed rewrites shared history and requires a force push.
cards.searchQuery: git commit amend last commit

cards.title: `git reset --soft`, `--mixed`, and `--hard HEAD~1`: what does each do to the index and working tree?
cards.body:
All three move the current branch back to `HEAD~1`; they differ in what else they reset.

- `--soft`: index and working tree untouched, so the undone commit's changes stay **staged**.
- `--mixed` (the default): index reset, working tree kept, so changes become **unstaged**.
- `--hard`: both reset; uncommitted changes to tracked files are discarded.

Watch out: `--hard` can destroy uncommitted work. Untracked files are not touched.
cards.searchQuery: git reset soft mixed hard difference

cards.title: Safest way to undo a commit that's already pushed to a shared branch, without rewriting history?
cards.body:
`git revert <commit>`

It makes a **new commit** that applies the inverse of that commit's changes. History is preserved, so collaborators aren't disrupted.

Watch out: `git reset` moves the branch pointer back, rewriting history. That is fine for local commits and harmful once pushed.
cards.searchQuery: git revert undo pushed commit safely

cards.title: Command to apply the changes from one specific commit on another branch onto your current branch?
cards.body:
`git cherry-pick <commit>`

It creates a new commit with the same changes and message but a **new hash**.

Example: port a bug fix from `main` to a release branch without merging everything else.
cards.searchQuery: git cherry-pick apply single commit

cards.title: What is `HEAD`, and what does it mean to be in 'detached HEAD' state?
cards.body:
`HEAD` is the ref for what you have checked out, normally a branch name. **Detached** means it points straight at a commit.

Normally the chain is `HEAD` to branch to commit. Detaching happens after `git checkout <hash>` or checking out a tag.

Watch out: new commits made while detached belong to no branch. Run `git switch -c <name>` before leaving, or they become hard to find.
cards.searchQuery: git detached HEAD state explained

cards.title: After a bad `git reset --hard`, which command lists where `HEAD` has recently pointed so you can recover lost commits?
cards.body:
`git reflog`

It records recent positions of `HEAD` (`HEAD@{0}`, `HEAD@{1}`, and so on). Recover with `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` or `git branch rescue <hash>`.

Watch out: the reflog is **local only**, and entries expire (90 days by default; 30 days for unreachable commits).
cards.searchQuery: git reflog recover lost commits

cards.title: Name the three areas a change passes through on its way into a commit.
cards.body:
The **working tree**, the **index** (staging area), and the **repository** (committed history).

`git add` copies changes from the working tree to the index. `git commit` turns the index into a new commit.

Key idea: a commit records the index, not the working tree, so unstaged edits are left out.
cards.searchQuery: git working tree index repository three areas

cards.title: Which command shows which files are staged, modified, or untracked?
cards.body:
`git status`

It lists staged changes, unstaged changes, and untracked files, plus how your branch compares with its upstream.

Tip: `git status -s` gives a compact two-column view.
cards.searchQuery: git status staged unstaged untracked files

cards.title: Which flag makes `git log` print one line per commit (abbreviated hash plus subject)?
cards.body:
`git log --oneline`

It is shorthand for `--pretty=oneline --abbrev-commit`.

Tip: add `--graph` (and `--all`) to see branch structure.
cards.searchQuery: git log oneline compact history

cards.title: Which `git log` flag draws an ASCII graph of branches and merges?
cards.body:
`--graph`

A common combination is `git log --oneline --graph --all`, which shows every branch.

Tip: without `--all`, only history reachable from the current branch is shown.
cards.searchQuery: git log graph branches merges ascii

cards.title: Which command (Git 2.23+) discards the unstaged edits to a file, restoring it from the index?
cards.body:
`git restore <file>`

The older equivalent is `git checkout -- <file>`.

Watch out: this overwrites your edits and they are **not recoverable**, because they were never committed or staged.
cards.searchQuery: git restore discard unstaged changes file

cards.title: Which command unstages a file but keeps your edits in the working tree?
cards.body:
`git restore --staged <file>`

The older equivalent is `git reset HEAD <file>`.

Key idea: the file's content in the working tree is untouched; only the index entry is reset to match `HEAD`.
cards.searchQuery: git restore staged unstage file keep changes

cards.title: Which command deletes a tracked file from the working tree and stages the deletion?
cards.body:
`git rm <file>`

The next commit then records the file as removed.

Tip: add `--cached` to remove the file from the index only, leaving it on disk.
cards.searchQuery: git rm remove tracked file stage deletion

cards.title: Which command renames or moves a tracked file and stages the change in one step?
cards.body:
`git mv <old> <new>`

It is equivalent to renaming the file yourself, then running `git rm` on the old path and `git add` on the new one.

Key idea: Git doesn't store renames explicitly; it detects them later by comparing file content similarity.
cards.searchQuery: git mv rename file stage

cards.title: In `.gitignore`, what does a trailing slash, as in `build/`, mean?
cards.body:
The pattern matches **directories only**, not files with that name.

A pattern without a slash, such as `*.log`, matches at any depth. A leading slash, as in `/build`, anchors the pattern to the `.gitignore` file's own directory.

Example: `/build` ignores only the top-level `build`, not `src/build`.
cards.searchQuery: gitignore trailing slash directory pattern

cards.title: In `.gitignore`, what does a leading `!` do, and what limits it?
cards.body:
It **re-includes** a path that an earlier pattern ignored.

```sh
*.log
!keep.log
```

Watch out: you can't re-include a file if one of its parent directories is itself ignored. Git never looks inside an excluded directory.
cards.searchQuery: gitignore negation exclamation re-include file

cards.title: Which command sets your commit author name for every repository on your account?
cards.body:
`git config --global user.name "Your Name"`

The email is set the same way with `user.email`. Both are recorded in every commit you make.

Tip: omit `--global` inside a repository to set a value for that repository only.
cards.searchQuery: git config global user.name set author

cards.title: Git reads config at three levels: system, global, local. Which has the highest precedence?
cards.body:
**Local** (the repository's `.git/config`).

More specific levels override broader ones: local beats global, and global beats system.

Example: set `user.email` globally for personal projects, then override it with a work address in one repository.
cards.searchQuery: git config system global local precedence

cards.title: A commit's hash is computed from its content. Which of these changes it: the message, the parent, the file contents?
cards.body:
All three.

The hash covers the commit's tree (file contents), its parent hash(es), author, committer, timestamps and message.

Why: that is why amending, rebasing or cherry-picking produces **new hashes**, and why changing old history changes every later hash.
cards.searchQuery: git commit hash computed from what content parent

cards.title: Name Git's four object types.
cards.body:
**Blob**, **tree**, **commit**, and **tag**.

A blob holds file content, a tree maps names to blobs and subtrees, a commit points to a tree and its parents, and an annotated tag points to another object.
cards.searchQuery: git object model blob tree commit tag

cards.title: In Git's object model, which object type maps file names to blobs (and to subtrees)?
cards.body:
tree

A blob stores only file **content**, with no name. The directory listing, with names and modes, lives in the tree.

Key idea: two files with identical content share one blob.
cards.searchQuery: git tree object maps file names to blobs

cards.title: Which option of `git add` lets you stage only chosen hunks of a file, one at a time?
cards.body:
`git add -p`

Git shows each hunk and asks `y`, `n`, `s` (split), or `e` (edit).

Tip: it's a good way to split unrelated changes in one file into separate, focused commits.
cards.searchQuery: git add patch stage hunks interactively

cards.title: Since Git 2.0, how does `git add -A` differ from `git add .` run inside a subdirectory?
cards.body:
`git add -A` stages changes across the **whole working tree**; `git add .` covers only the current directory and below.

Both stage new, modified, and deleted files within their scope.

Watch out: either one can stage files you didn't mean to, such as secrets or build output. Check with `git status` first.
cards.searchQuery: git add -A vs git add dot difference

cards.title: What does `git commit -a` stage automatically, and what does it skip?
cards.body:
It stages **modified and deleted tracked files**, and skips **untracked** files.

So `git commit -am "msg"` is a shortcut for `git add -u` followed by `git commit -m "msg"`.

Watch out: a brand-new file still needs an explicit `git add`.
cards.searchQuery: git commit -a stage tracked files skip untracked

cards.title: By convention, in which grammatical mood is a commit subject line written?
cards.body:
imperative

Write it as a command, such as 'Fix null check in parser', so it completes the sentence 'If applied, this commit will ...'.

Tip: keep the subject short (around 50 characters), leave a blank line, then explain the why in the body.
cards.searchQuery: git commit message imperative mood convention

cards.title: Which command displays one commit's metadata, message, and diff?
cards.body:
`git show <commit>`

With no argument it shows `HEAD`.

Tip: `git show <commit>:<path>` prints a file as it was in that commit.
cards.searchQuery: git show commit message and diff

cards.title: What is the difference between `HEAD~2` and `HEAD^2`?
cards.body:
`HEAD~2` is the **grandparent** (first parent, twice). `HEAD^2` is the **second parent** of a merge commit.

`~n` walks back n generations along first parents. `^n` selects the n-th parent of a single commit.

Example: for a merge commit `M`, `M^1` is the branch you merged into and `M^2` is the branch you merged in.
cards.searchQuery: git HEAD~ vs HEAD^ tilde caret difference

cards.title: What does `git diff main...feature` (three dots) compare?
cards.body:
The tip of `feature` against the **merge base** of `main` and `feature`.

It shows what changed on `feature` since the branches diverged, ignoring newer work on `main`.

Watch out: `git diff main..feature` (two dots) compares the two tips directly.
cards.searchQuery: git diff three dots merge base branch changes

cards.title: Which commits does `git log main..feature` list?
cards.body:
Commits reachable from `feature` but **not** from `main`.

That is the work on `feature` that `main` doesn't have yet.

Tip: `git log origin/main..HEAD` lists your unpushed commits.
cards.searchQuery: git log double dot range commits not in branch

cards.title: What is a Git branch, physically?
cards.body:
A lightweight, movable **pointer** to a commit.

Committing on a branch moves that pointer forward to the new commit. `HEAD` normally points at the current branch.

Key idea: creating a branch copies no files, so branching is nearly free.
cards.searchQuery: git branch is a pointer to a commit

cards.title: Which command deletes a local branch, but refuses if it has unmerged commits?
cards.body:
`git branch -d <name>`

Use `-D` (force) to delete it even if unmerged.

Watch out: you can't delete the branch you're on. Switch away first. Commits on a force-deleted branch can usually be found with `git reflog`.
cards.searchQuery: git branch -d delete merged local branch

cards.title: Which command lists the local branches already merged into the current branch?
cards.body:
`git branch --merged`

These are usually safe to delete. `git branch --no-merged` lists the opposite.

Tip: use it to clean up old feature branches after merging.
cards.searchQuery: git branch --merged list merged branches

cards.title: Which command renames the current local branch to `new-name`?
cards.body:
`git branch -m new-name`

Give two names (`git branch -m old new`) to rename a different branch.

Watch out: this renames only the local branch. A branch already pushed keeps its old name on the remote until you push the new one and delete the old.
cards.searchQuery: git branch -m rename current branch

cards.title: Which flag makes `git branch` list local and remote-tracking branches together?
cards.body:
`git branch -a`

Remote-tracking branches appear as `remotes/origin/main` and similar. `git branch -r` lists only those.

Key idea: remote-tracking branches reflect your last fetch, not the live state of the remote.
cards.searchQuery: git branch -a list remote and local branches

cards.title: Which command jumps back to the branch you were on before the current one?
cards.body:
`git switch -`

The older form is `git checkout -`.

Tip: it works like `cd -` in a shell, so you can toggle between two branches quickly.
cards.searchQuery: git switch - previous branch shortcut

cards.title: Which `git merge` flag forces a merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible?
cards.body:
`--no-ff`

The merge commit marks where a feature branch was integrated, keeping the branch visible in history.

Watch out: the setting `merge.ff=false` makes this the default for every merge.
cards.searchQuery: git merge --no-ff force merge commit

cards.title: What does `git merge --squash feature` do?
cards.body:
It applies all of `feature`'s changes to the index and working tree but **does not commit**.

You then run `git commit` to record one ordinary commit. No merge relationship is recorded, because the new commit has a single parent.

Watch out: Git won't remember that `feature` was merged, so `git branch -d feature` complains and you must use `-D`.
cards.searchQuery: git merge --squash single commit no merge parent

cards.title: Which command cancels a merge that stopped on conflicts and restores the pre-merge state?
cards.body:
`git merge --abort`

It works while the merge is still in progress, before you commit.

Tip: rebase has its own `git rebase --abort`, and cherry-pick has `git cherry-pick --abort`.
cards.searchQuery: git merge --abort cancel merge conflicts

cards.title: A three-way merge compares which three commits?
cards.body:
The two **branch tips** and their **merge base** (most recent common ancestor).

For each region, Git takes the side that changed relative to the base. If both sides changed the same lines differently, you get a conflict.

Why: without the base, Git couldn't tell whether a difference is an addition on one side or a deletion on the other.
cards.searchQuery: git three-way merge merge base two tips

cards.title: Which command prints the best common ancestor of two branches?
cards.body:
`git merge-base <a> <b>`

This is the commit where the histories diverged, and the base used by a three-way merge.

Example: `git merge-base main feature` gives the starting point of `feature`'s work.
cards.searchQuery: git merge-base best common ancestor

cards.title: You are on `feature` and run `git rebase main`. What happens?
cards.body:
Git replays `feature`'s commits, one by one, on top of the current tip of `main`.

The replayed commits are **new commits** with new hashes; the originals are abandoned. The result is a linear history.

Watch out: you may have to resolve conflicts once per replayed commit.
cards.searchQuery: git rebase main replay commits onto branch

cards.title: You resolved a conflict during a rebase and staged the file. Which command moves the rebase on?
cards.body:
`git rebase --continue`

It creates the commit for you and replays the next one.

Watch out: don't run `git commit` yourself in the middle of a rebase (except when editing a commit on purpose); use `--continue`.
cards.searchQuery: git rebase --continue after resolving conflict

cards.title: Which command cancels a rebase in progress and returns the branch to how it was before?
cards.body:
`git rebase --abort`

The branch goes back to its original commits, as if you never started.

Tip: use it when a rebase produces more conflicts than you expected, then try a merge instead.
cards.searchQuery: git rebase --abort cancel rebase

cards.title: Command to interactively edit, reorder, squash, or drop your last 3 commits?
cards.body:
`git rebase -i HEAD~3`

Git opens a todo list with one line per commit. Change the word at the start of a line (`pick`, `reword`, `edit`, `squash`, `fixup`, `drop`) or reorder the lines.

Watch out: it rewrites those commits, so avoid it on commits you've already shared.
cards.searchQuery: git rebase -i interactive squash reorder commits

cards.title: In an interactive rebase, how does `squash` differ from `fixup`?
cards.body:
Both fold a commit into the one above it. `squash` lets you **edit the combined message**; `fixup` **discards** the folded commit's message.

Example: use `fixup` for a 'typo' commit and `squash` when both messages are worth keeping.

Tip: `git commit --fixup <commit>` marks a commit for automatic folding later.
cards.searchQuery: git rebase squash vs fixup difference

cards.title: What does `git rebase --onto main topicA topicB` do?
cards.body:
It takes the commits in `topicA..topicB` and replays them onto `main`.

That is, the commits on `topicB` that are not on `topicA`.

Example: `topicB` was branched from `topicA`, but you want it to start from `main` without bringing `topicA`'s commits along.
cards.searchQuery: git rebase --onto transplant branch commits

cards.title: Which command fetches and then rebases your local commits onto the upstream branch, instead of merging?
cards.body:
`git pull --rebase`

It avoids the extra merge commit that a plain `git pull` creates when your branch and upstream have diverged.

Tip: set it as the default with `git config pull.rebase true`.
cards.searchQuery: git pull --rebase instead of merge

cards.title: Which `git pull` option refuses to proceed unless the update is a pure fast-forward?
cards.body:
`git pull --ff-only`

If your branch and upstream have diverged, it stops with an error instead of creating a merge commit or rebasing.

Tip: it is a safe default, and you then choose between merge and rebase deliberately.
cards.searchQuery: git pull --ff-only fast-forward only

cards.title: During a merge, what are 'ours' and 'theirs' in `git checkout --ours <file>`?
cards.body:
'Ours' is the **current branch's** version; 'theirs' is the **incoming** branch's version.

So `git checkout --theirs <file>` takes the whole file from the branch being merged in.

Watch out: during a rebase the meanings swap. 'Ours' is the branch you're rebasing onto, and 'theirs' is your commit being replayed.
cards.searchQuery: git checkout --ours --theirs merge conflict

cards.title: Which command lists your configured remotes together with their URLs?
cards.body:
`git remote -v`

Each remote is shown twice: once for fetch and once for push.

Key idea: a remote is just a named URL, and `origin` is the conventional name for the one you cloned from.
cards.searchQuery: git remote -v list remotes urls

cards.title: Which command adds a remote named `origin` pointing at a URL?
cards.body:
`git remote add origin <url>`

It only records the name and URL; nothing is downloaded until you fetch or push.

Tip: use `git remote set-url origin <url>` to change the URL later.
cards.searchQuery: git remote add origin url

cards.title: Command to push the new local branch `feature` to `origin` and set it as the branch's upstream?
cards.body:
`git push -u origin feature`

The `-u` flag (`--set-upstream`) links the local branch to `origin/feature`, so later `git pull` and `git push` need no arguments.

Tip: `git branch -vv` shows each branch's upstream.
cards.searchQuery: git push -u set upstream new branch

cards.title: What is `origin/main`?
cards.body:
A **remote-tracking branch**: a local, read-only bookmark of where `main` was on `origin` at your last fetch.

You can't commit to it directly. `git fetch` moves it, and `git pull` fetches then integrates it into your current branch.

Watch out: it can be stale; it doesn't update until you fetch.
cards.searchQuery: git remote-tracking branch origin/main meaning

cards.title: Which push option force-pushes only if the remote branch is still where you last fetched it?
cards.body:
`git push --force-with-lease`

It refuses to overwrite commits you haven't seen, such as a teammate's push made after your last fetch.

Why: plain `--force` overwrites the remote branch unconditionally and can silently destroy others' work.
cards.searchQuery: git push --force-with-lease safer force push

cards.title: Which option makes `git fetch` delete remote-tracking branches whose branch no longer exists on the remote?
cards.body:
`git fetch --prune`

It removes stale entries such as `origin/old-feature` after that branch was deleted on the remote.

Watch out: it does not delete your **local** branches, only the remote-tracking ones.
cards.searchQuery: git fetch --prune remove stale remote branches

cards.title: Command to delete the branch `feature` on the remote `origin`?
cards.body:
`git push origin --delete feature`

The older form is `git push origin :feature`, which pushes 'nothing' to that branch name.

Watch out: this does not delete your local `feature` branch; use `git branch -d feature` for that.
cards.searchQuery: git push origin --delete remote branch

cards.title: Which command lists local branches with their upstream and how far ahead or behind each is?
cards.body:
`git branch -vv`

Output includes the upstream, such as `[origin/main: ahead 2, behind 1]`.

Tip: it reflects your last fetch, so run `git fetch` first for current numbers.
cards.searchQuery: git branch -vv upstream ahead behind

cards.title: Which command clones a repository with only the latest commit of history?
cards.body:
`git clone --depth 1 <url>`

This **shallow clone** is much smaller and faster, which is handy in CI.

Watch out: history is truncated, so log, blame, and some merges are limited. `git fetch --unshallow` restores the full history.
cards.searchQuery: git clone --depth 1 shallow clone

cards.title: `git push` is rejected as 'non-fast-forward'. What does that mean, and what is the usual fix?
cards.body:
The remote branch has commits you don't have locally, so pushing would drop them.

Fetch, integrate with `git pull` (merge) or `git pull --rebase`, resolve any conflicts, then push again.

Watch out: forcing the push is rarely the right fix on a shared branch.
cards.searchQuery: git push rejected non-fast-forward fix

cards.title: Which Git setting chooses the name of the initial branch created by `git init`?
cards.body:
`init.defaultBranch`

Example: `git config --global init.defaultBranch main`.

Tip: `git init -b main` sets the name for a single repository.
cards.searchQuery: git init.defaultBranch config initial branch name

cards.title: Command to undo your last commit but keep its changes staged?
cards.body:
`git reset --soft HEAD~1`

The branch moves back one commit; the index and working tree stay as they were.

Tip: you can now edit the staged changes and commit again with a better message or split the commit.
cards.searchQuery: git reset --soft HEAD~1 undo last commit keep staged

cards.title: After `git reset --hard`, which work can the reflog NOT bring back?
cards.body:
Uncommitted changes to tracked files.

The reflog tracks commits. Edits that were never committed (or at least staged) have no commit to point to.

Watch out: committed work is recoverable with `git reflog`; untouched untracked files simply stay where they are.
cards.searchQuery: git reset --hard uncommitted changes lost reflog

cards.title: Which flag of `git clean` shows what would be deleted without deleting anything?
cards.body:
`-n` (long form `--dry-run`)

`git clean` deletes **untracked** files. By default it refuses to run without `-f`, and it skips directories unless you add `-d`.

Watch out: deleted untracked files are gone for good, so run `git clean -n` first.
cards.searchQuery: git clean -n dry run untracked files

cards.title: Reverting a merge commit needs an option naming the parent to keep. Which command reverts a merge `M` back to its first parent?
cards.body:
`git revert -m 1 <M>`

The `-m 1` option says the first parent (the branch you merged **into**) is the mainline, so the changes brought in by the other side are undone.

Watch out: re-merging that branch later won't bring those changes back, because Git thinks they're already merged. Revert the revert first.
cards.searchQuery: git revert merge commit -m 1 mainline parent

cards.title: Which `git revert` flag applies the inverse changes to the working tree and index without creating a commit?
cards.body:
`--no-commit` (short form `-n`)

It lets you revert several commits and record them as one commit.

Example: `git revert -n A B` then a single `git commit`.
cards.searchQuery: git revert --no-commit combine reverts one commit

cards.title: Command to shelve your uncommitted changes to tracked files and get a clean working tree?
cards.body:
`git stash`

It saves the changes on a stack and resets the working tree to `HEAD`. Bring them back later with `git stash pop`.

Example: you're mid-change when an urgent fix comes in. Stash, fix and commit, then pop.
cards.searchQuery: git stash save uncommitted changes

cards.title: Which command lists all your stash entries?
cards.body:
`git stash list`

Entries are named `stash@{0}` (newest), `stash@{1}`, and so on.

Tip: `git stash show -p stash@{0}` shows what an entry contains.
cards.searchQuery: git stash list entries

cards.title: Which command stashes your tracked changes and your new untracked files too?
cards.body:
`git stash -u`

Long form: `--include-untracked`. A plain `git stash` leaves untracked files in place.

Watch out: ignored files are skipped even with `-u`; add `-a` (`--all`) to include them as well.
cards.searchQuery: git stash -u include untracked files

cards.title: Command to stash your changes with a descriptive label?
cards.body:
`git stash push -m "message"`

The message appears in `git stash list`, which helps when you have several entries.

Tip: add `-u` to include untracked files in the same stash.
cards.searchQuery: git stash push -m named stash message

cards.title: What name refers to the second most recent stash entry, e.g. in `git stash apply <name>`?
cards.body:
`stash@{1}`

The newest entry is `stash@{0}`, so numbering counts back from there.

Watch out: dropping or popping an entry renumbers the ones behind it.
cards.searchQuery: git stash apply stash@{1} specific entry

cards.title: Command to add newly staged changes to the last commit while keeping its message?
cards.body:
`git commit --amend --no-edit`

The commit gets the staged changes added and a new hash, but the message stays the same.

Watch out: don't amend commits you've already pushed to a shared branch.
cards.searchQuery: git commit --amend --no-edit keep message

cards.title: How do you restore one file to its content from two commits ago, without moving the branch?
cards.body:
`git restore --source=HEAD~2 <file>`

It overwrites the working-tree copy with the version from `HEAD~2`. Add `--staged` to restore the index copy too.

Key idea: unlike `git reset`, this changes files only; no branch moves.
cards.searchQuery: git restore --source restore file from older commit

cards.title: After a merge you regret (and haven't made new commits), which command undoes it using `ORIG_HEAD`?
cards.body:
`git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD`

Git sets `ORIG_HEAD` to the previous `HEAD` before risky operations such as merge, rebase, and reset.

Watch out: `--hard` also discards uncommitted changes, so commit or stash first.
cards.searchQuery: git ORIG_HEAD undo merge reset hard

cards.title: Of `git reset <commit>` and `git restore <file>`, which one moves the current branch pointer?
cards.body:
`git reset`

It moves the branch (and, depending on mode, resets the index and working tree). `git restore` only changes files in the index or working tree.

Tip: use `restore` to undo file edits and `reset` to undo commits.
cards.searchQuery: git reset vs git restore branch pointer

cards.title: Which `git tag` flag creates an annotated tag (with tagger, date, and message) rather than a lightweight one?
cards.body:
`-a`

Example: `git tag -a v1.0 -m "Release 1.0"`. Annotated tags are full objects in the repository.

Tip: `git tag` with a bare name, such as `git tag v1.0`, makes a lightweight tag.
cards.searchQuery: git tag -a annotated tag create

cards.title: `git push` does not send tags by default. Which option pushes all your local tags?
cards.body:
`git push --tags`

To send just one tag, name it: `git push origin v1.0`.

Watch out: `--tags` also pushes lightweight tags you may have made by accident.
cards.searchQuery: git push --tags push all tags to remote

cards.title: Which command names a commit as the nearest tag plus commits since, plus a short hash (like `v1.2-5-g3a1b2c3`)?
cards.body:
`git describe`

In `v1.2-5-g3a1b2c3`, the nearest tag is `v1.2`, there are 5 commits since it, and `g3a1b2c3` is `g` (for git) plus the abbreviated hash.

Tip: it's often used to build version strings.
cards.searchQuery: git describe nearest tag version string

cards.title: Which command shows, line by line, which commit and author last changed each line of a file?
cards.body:
`git blame <file>`

Use it to find out why a line is the way it is, then `git show <commit>` for the full context.

Tip: `-L 10,20` limits the output to lines 10 to 20.
cards.searchQuery: git blame line by line author commit

cards.title: Which command binary-searches history to find the commit that introduced a bug?
cards.body:
`git bisect`

You mark one commit `bad` and one older commit `good`; Git checks out midpoints and you answer `good` or `bad` until it names the first bad commit.

Example: about 10 steps cover 1,000 commits, since each step halves the range.

Tip: finish with `git bisect reset`.
cards.searchQuery: git bisect binary search find bug commit

cards.title: Which `git log` option finds commits that added or removed occurrences of a given string?
cards.body:
`-S<string>`, called the **pickaxe**.

Example: `git log -S"parseConfig"` lists commits where the number of occurrences of `parseConfig` changed.

Tip: `-G<regex>` matches changed lines against a regular expression instead.
cards.searchQuery: git log -S pickaxe search history for string

cards.title: Which `git log` flag keeps following a single file's history across renames?
cards.body:
`--follow`

Example: `git log --follow -- <file>`.

Watch out: it works for one file at a time. Without it, history stops at the commit where the file was renamed.
cards.searchQuery: git log --follow file history across renames

cards.title: Which command searches the content of tracked files in the working tree?
cards.body:
`git grep <pattern>`

It only searches tracked files, so it skips ignored build output, and it is usually faster than plain `grep -r`.

Tip: add a commit, as in `git grep <pattern> v1.0`, to search an older version.
cards.searchQuery: git grep search tracked files

cards.title: Which `git diff` option lists only the names of changed files?
cards.body:
`--name-only`

Example: `git diff --name-only main` lists files that differ from `main`.

Tip: `--stat` adds a per-file summary of lines added and removed.
cards.searchQuery: git diff --name-only list changed files

cards.title: In which directory does Git look for hook scripts such as `pre-commit` by default?
cards.body:
`.git/hooks`

A `pre-commit` hook that exits with a non-zero status aborts the commit. `git commit --no-verify` skips it.

Watch out: files under `.git` aren't versioned or cloned. To share hooks, keep them in the repo and point `core.hooksPath` at that folder.
cards.searchQuery: git hooks pre-commit .git/hooks directory

cards.title: Which command checks out another branch into a second directory, sharing the same repository?
cards.body:
`git worktree add <path> <branch>`

You can work on a hotfix in a second folder without stashing or switching in your main one.

Watch out: a branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time.
cards.searchQuery: git worktree add second working directory

cards.title: What does a repository record for a Git submodule?
cards.body:
The submodule's **URL and path** in `.gitmodules`, plus a pointer to one **specific commit** of the submodule repository.

Watch out: pulling the parent doesn't move the submodule's checkout. Run `git submodule update` to match the recorded commit.
cards.searchQuery: git submodule records commit pointer gitmodules

cards.title: Which flag makes `git clone` also fetch and check out the repository's submodules?
cards.body:
`--recurse-submodules`

Without it, submodule folders are cloned empty. Fix an existing clone with `git submodule update --init`.
cards.searchQuery: git clone --recurse-submodules fetch submodules

cards.title: Which command cancels a cherry-pick that stopped on a conflict?
cards.body:
`git cherry-pick --abort`

It returns the branch to its state before the cherry-pick began.

Tip: to finish instead, resolve the conflict, `git add` the files, and run `git cherry-pick --continue`.
cards.searchQuery: git cherry-pick --abort conflict cancel

cards.title: How many parents does an ordinary two-branch merge commit have?
cards.body:
2

The first parent is the branch you merged into; the second is the tip of the branch you merged in.

Key idea: ordinary commits have 1 parent, and a repository's root commit has none.
cards.searchQuery: git merge commit two parents

cards.title: Which hidden directory at a repository's root holds its entire history and configuration?
cards.body:
.git

It contains the object database, refs, `HEAD`, and local config. The files outside it are just the working tree.

Watch out: deleting `.git` removes all history, leaving only the current files.
cards.searchQuery: what is the .git directory contains
